## Code Status

Merged on 2026-11-17 from `candidate_methods.qmd`, sections 3 to 5 of `final_checks.qmd`
and Part B of `robustness_analyses.qmd` (now in `scripts/archive/`). The code is
unchanged apart from object names that would otherwise clash, and each section that
draws random numbers re-sets the seed so its results match the original script exactly.
Not yet rendered on the real data.

## Purpose

Feeds Section 7.9 of the capstone write-up (candidate methods under the variety
standard), plus the stricter-exclusion check in Section 7.11.

1.  **Methods** and **which methods qualify** under the variety standard.
2.  **Held-out scores** for every candidate, on pooled styles and on informal messages
    only (Table 20).
3.  **The ceiling**: how high any qualifying method could score (Table 19).
4.  **Selecting a method**, whether the preference-based methods **personalize**, and
    **paired comparisons** between candidates (Table 21).
5.  **Method refinements**: how tied preferences and the norms rule are handled
    (Tables 23 and 24), and results by preference pattern.
6.  **Fairness**: who benefits under each method, with tests (Table 22).
7.  **Selection stability**, a **normality check** for the "worse off" metric, and
    **stricter exclusion**.

## The Variety Standard

A method qualifies only if, for **every** respondent:

-   they receive at least `min_tones` tones (3), and
-   their least-seen tone makes up at least `min_share` of messages (20%).

Together these cap the most-seen tone at 60% (60/20/20).

## Setup

```{r}
#| label: Setup
# Load packages and this study's functions, then read the cleaned panel in long format
# (one row per message rating). The seed makes the cross-validation folds and bootstrap
# resamples repeatable.
options(conflicts.policy = "depends.ok")
library(tidyverse)

source("https://github.com/jjcurtin/lab_support/blob/main/format_path.R?raw=true")
source(here::here("scripts", "functions_llmpanel.R"))
source(here::here("scripts", "functions_assignment.R"))

path_processed <- format_path("llmpanel/data_processed")

raw_panel <- read_csv(here::here(path_processed, "panel.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
panel_long <- format_eda(raw_panel, long = TRUE)

# tone_levels and pref_cols are defined in functions_llmpanel.R

set.seed(102030)
```

*Settings*

```{r}
#| label: Settings
# Variety standard
min_tones <- 3
min_share <- 0.20

# Selection rule (Section 5): among qualifying methods within `margin` points of
# the best qualifying method's held-out mean, prefer the one that leaves the
# fewest people worse off than an even rotation.
margin <- 0.03

# "Clearly worse off": a true expected rating at least this far below what the
# person would get from an even rotation of all five tones
harm_threshold <- 0.25

# Held-out scoring: repeated k-fold over respondents
cv_repeats <- 6
cv_folds <- 5
n_boot <- 2000
n_sim <- 100000
```

*Preferences (one row per respondent, in a fixed order used throughout)*

```{r}
#| label: Preferences
prefs <- prep_preferences(panel_long)
pref_wide <- prefs$pref_wide
ids <- prefs$ids
n <- prefs$n
P <- prefs$P
pref_by_tone <- prefs$pref_by_tone
```

*Ratings for each style setting*

For each setting this builds the respondent-by-tone matrix of mean ratings and
fits a mixed model that separates stable person-by-tone differences
(`sd_person_tone`) from message-level noise (`sd_resid`). Both are needed for
the noise-corrected metrics.

```{r}
#| label: Style Data
# prep_style() is in functions_assignment.R
style_data <- list(
  "Pooled styles" = prep_style("both"),
  "Informal only" = prep_style("informal"))

map(style_data, \(s) s[c("n_per_tone", "sd_person_tone", "sd_resid")]) |>
  map(as_tibble) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "styles")
```

# 1. Methods

Each method is a function that returns a weight for every tone for each
respondent. `top` is the tones ranked by mean rating **among training
respondents only**, so nothing about a held-out respondent's ratings decides
what they receive.

**Fixed methods** give everyone the same weights. **Preference-based methods**
use each person's own stated preferences:

-   **Own order.** Everyone gets the sample's top three tones, but the weights
    (e.g. 50/30/20) follow the person's own preference order among those
    three. Tied tones share their weights (a tie for first gives 40/40/20; all
    three tied gives equal thirds).
-   **Sample tiebreak.** A variant of own order in which tied tones are
    ordered by the sample ranking instead of sharing their weights. Someone
    with no stated order among the three tones gets the fixed 50/30/20
    rotation; someone with a full order is unaffected. Added because the
    shared-weights version scored below a fixed rotation for people who tied
    its three tones.
-   **Own order + norms.** As above, but a person who put norms in their
    highest preference tier gets norms in place of the sample's third tone.
    This uses the finding that a norms preference is informative.
-   **Own top three.** The person's own three most-preferred tones, weighted
    by their preference order. The sample is used only to break ties. This is
    the candidate that leans least on what the sample as a whole liked.
-   **Rule-based.** The five rules from `methods_first_round.qmd`
    (`data_driven_weights()`).

```{r}
#| label: Method Definitions
# fixed(), own_order() and own_top_three() are in functions_assignment.R

# Rule-based weights do not depend on the training sample
rule_wide <- data_driven_weights(pref_by_tone) |>
  select(subid, tone, weight) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = tone, values_from = weight) |>
  arrange(subid)
stopifnot(identical(rule_wide$subid, ids))
W_rule <- as.matrix(rule_wide[, tone_levels])
rule_based <- function(top, rows) W_rule[rows, , drop = FALSE]

methods <- list(
  # Reference methods that do not meet the variety standard
  "Mean-only"                       = fixed(1),
  "Top two, equal"                  = fixed(c(.5, .5)),
  "Top three, 45/45/10"             = fixed(c(.45, .45, .10)),
  # Fixed candidates
  "Top three, 60/20/20"             = fixed(c(.60, .20, .20)),
  "Top three, 50/30/20"             = fixed(c(.50, .30, .20)),
  "Top three, 50/25/25"             = fixed(c(.50, .25, .25)),
  "Top three, 40/40/20"             = fixed(c(.40, .40, .20)),
  "Top three, 40/30/30"             = fixed(c(.40, .30, .30)),
  "Top three, equal"                = fixed(rep(1 / 3, 3)),
  "Top four, 40/20/20/20"           = fixed(c(.40, .20, .20, .20)),
  "Top four, 30/30/20/20"           = fixed(c(.30, .30, .20, .20)),
  "Top four, equal"                 = fixed(rep(1 / 4, 4)),
  "Uniform (all five)"              = fixed(rep(1 / 5, 5)),
  # Preference-based candidates
  "Own order, 50/30/20"             = own_order(c(.50, .30, .20)),
  "Own order, 40/40/20"             = own_order(c(.40, .40, .20)),
  "Own order, 50/30/20 + norms"     = own_order(c(.50, .30, .20), norms = "tier"),
  "Own order, 50/30/20, sample tiebreak" =
    own_order(c(.50, .30, .20), ties = "sample"),
  "Own order, 50/30/20 + norms, sample tiebreak" =
    own_order(c(.50, .30, .20), norms = "tier", ties = "sample"),
  "Own top three, 50/30/20"         = own_top_three(c(.50, .30, .20)),
  "Rule-based"                      = rule_based)
```

# 2. Which Methods Qualify?

Checked on every respondent, with tones ranked on the full sample (pooled
styles). A method qualifies only if 100% of respondents meet both parts of the
standard.

```{r}
#| label: Variety Check
top_full <- names(sort(colMeans(style_data[["Pooled styles"]]$M), decreasing = TRUE))
top_full

variety <- imap(methods, \(f, nm) {
  W <- f(top_full, seq_len(n))
  n_tones <- rowSums(W > 0)
  least <- apply(W, 1, \(w) min(w[w > 0]))
  ok <- n_tones >= min_tones & least >= min_share - 1e-9
  tibble(method = nm,
         tones_min = min(n_tones), tones_max = max(n_tones),
         least_seen_share = min(least),
         most_seen_share = max(W),
         pct_respondents_meeting = mean(ok),
         qualifies = all(ok))
}) |> list_rbind()

variety |> arrange(desc(qualifies), desc(most_seen_share)) |> print(n = Inf)
qualifying <- variety$method[variety$qualifies]
```

Methods from earlier scripts that are not carried forward, and why:

-   **Mean-only, top two, 45/45/10:** fewer than three tones or a tone under 20%.
-   **Drop own least-preferred tone(s):** ties drop several tones at once, so
    some respondents are left with one or two tones.
-   **Tier-, power- and score-weighted individualized methods:** the least-seen
    tone falls below 20% for many respondents.
-   **30/30/20/10/10:** two tones at 10%.

# 3. Held-Out Scores, Pooled and Informal

Each respondent is scored only in folds where they were not used to rank the
tones. No configuration is being tuned here, so one level of cross-validation
is enough; the nested version in `methods_heldout.qmd` is for selecting among
configurations. The same folds are used for both style settings.

```{r}
#| label: Folds
# Re-set the seed: these folds are the first random draw, as in the original script
set.seed(102030)
folds <- make_respondent_folds(n, cv_folds, cv_repeats)
length(folds)
```

## Metrics

For each method and respondent, the **gain** is their expected rating under
the method minus what they would get from an even rotation of all five tones.
An even rotation is the natural "no decision made" baseline.

-   `held_out_mean`: mean expected rating.
-   `retained`: the method's mean gain as a share of mean-only's gain. 100%
    means as helpful on average as giving everyone the single best tone.
-   `diff_vs_mean_only` with a paired 95% bootstrap interval.
-   `sd_gain`: how much the gain truly varies between people, after removing
    rating noise.
-   `pct_worse_off`: estimated share of people whose **true** expected rating
    under the method is below their even-rotation baseline.
-   `pct_clearly_worse`: the same, for at least `harm_threshold` points below.

**Why these replace the optimization and disadvantage rates.** The old rates
ask how often a person gets their single best or worst tone. That label is
unreliable (a person's best tone in two contexts is among their worst in the
third about 44% of the time), it is inflated by ties, and the rates rise and
fall with mean helpfulness, so they do not pull against it. The metrics here
measure the same concern, who is left worse off, on the rating scale, and they
do pull against mean helpfulness: concentrating on one tone raises the average
but widens the spread of who gains and who loses.

**How the noise correction works.** A respondent's observed gain is their true
gain plus rating noise. The noise variance is known from the mixed model
(`sd_resid`^2 / messages per tone, times the sum of squared differences between
the method's weights and an even 20%). Subtracting it from the observed
variance of gains leaves the true variance. The share worse off then comes
from a normal distribution with the observed mean gain and the true SD. This
assumes true gains are roughly normal.

```{r}
#| label: Evaluate
# Score every method for one style setting: held-out weights and expected ratings from
# evaluate_methods() (functions_assignment.R), then the summary table with bootstrap
# intervals and the noise-corrected worse-off shares
score_style <- function(s) {
  # Each respondent's weights, averaged over the repeats in which they were held out
  e <- evaluate_methods(methods, s$M, folds, cv_repeats)
  W_bar <- e$weights
  value_mat <- e$values
  uniform_value <- e$uniform

  boot_means <- map(seq_len(n_boot), \(i) {
    colMeans(value_mat[sample(n, replace = TRUE), , drop = FALSE])
  }) |> do.call(what = rbind)
  boot_diff <- boot_means - boot_means[, "Mean-only"]

  gain_mean_only <- mean(value_mat[, "Mean-only"] - uniform_value)

  imap(W_bar, \(W, nm) {
    v <- value_mat[, nm]
    gain <- v - uniform_value
    noise_var <- s$sd_resid^2 / s$n_per_tone * rowSums((W - 1 / length(tone_levels))^2)
    true_sd <- sqrt(max(var(gain) - mean(noise_var), 0))
    is_uniform <- all(abs(W - 1 / length(tone_levels)) < 1e-9)
    tibble(
      method = nm,
      held_out_mean = mean(v),
      retained = mean(gain) / gain_mean_only,
      diff_vs_mean_only = mean(v) - mean(value_mat[, "Mean-only"]),
      diff_low = quantile(boot_diff[, nm], .025),
      diff_high = quantile(boot_diff[, nm], .975),
      sd_gain = if (is_uniform) 0 else true_sd,
      pct_worse_off = if (is_uniform || true_sd == 0) NA_real_ else
        pnorm(0, mean(gain), true_sd),
      pct_clearly_worse = if (is_uniform || true_sd == 0) NA_real_ else
        pnorm(-harm_threshold, mean(gain), true_sd),
      # not noise-corrected, for comparison only
      pct_worse_off_raw = if (is_uniform) NA_real_ else mean(gain < 0))
  }) |>
    list_rbind() |>
    mutate(qualifies = method %in% qualifying, .after = method) -> summary_tbl

  list(summary = summary_tbl, values = value_mat, weights = W_bar,
       uniform = uniform_value,
       # used by method_metrics() in Sections 8 to 11
       sd_resid = s$sd_resid, n_per_tone = s$n_per_tone)
}

evaluated <- map(style_data, score_style)
results <- map(evaluated, "summary")
```

## Candidate Comparison

All methods, pooled styles first. Rows that do not qualify are kept as
reference points.

```{r}
#| label: Results Pooled
results[["Pooled styles"]] |>
  arrange(desc(qualifies), desc(held_out_mean)) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3))) |>
  print(n = Inf, width = Inf)
```

```{r}
#| label: Results Informal
# The same table scored on informal messages only: methods that meet the variety
# standard first, then by held-out mean
results[["Informal only"]] |>
  arrange(desc(qualifies), desc(held_out_mean)) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3))) |>
  print(n = Inf, width = Inf)
```

## Pooled vs. Informal, Side by Side

If style does not matter for choosing tones, the two columns should rank the
methods the same way, with informal means a little higher throughout. The
pooled figures rest on twice as many messages per tone.

```{r}
#| label: Side by Side
side_by_side <- inner_join(
  results[["Pooled styles"]] |>
    select(method, qualifies, mean_pooled = held_out_mean, retained_pooled = retained,
           worse_pooled = pct_worse_off),
  results[["Informal only"]] |>
    select(method, mean_informal = held_out_mean, retained_informal = retained,
           worse_informal = pct_worse_off),
  by = "method") |>
  mutate(rank_pooled = min_rank(desc(mean_pooled)),
         rank_informal = min_rank(desc(mean_informal))) |>
  arrange(rank_pooled)

side_by_side |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3))) |>
  print(n = Inf, width = Inf)

# Agreement between the two rankings
cor(side_by_side$mean_pooled, side_by_side$mean_informal, method = "spearman")
```

```{r}
#| label: Trade-off Plot
# Trade-off plot: held-out mean helpfulness (x) against the share of people worse off
# than an even rotation (y), one panel per style setting. Green points meet the
# variety standard.
results |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "styles") |>
  filter(!is.na(pct_worse_off)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = held_out_mean, y = pct_worse_off, color = qualifies)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = method), size = 3, vjust = -0.8, check_overlap = TRUE,
            show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~styles, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "forestgreen", `FALSE` = "grey50"),
                     labels = c(`TRUE` = "Meets variety standard", `FALSE` = "Does not")) +
  labs(x = "Held-out mean helpfulness",
       y = "Estimated share worse off than an even rotation",
       color = NULL,
       subtitle = "Best methods are toward the bottom right") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

# 4. The Ceiling: Is 5.5 Reachable?

How high could a method score? Simulating people from the mixed model (shared
tone means plus a stable personal deviation for each tone) gives the value of
several ideals:

-   **Oracle, no constraint:** every message in the person's true best tone.
    This is the noise-free version of the "best case" (about 5.8 in-sample).
-   **Oracle under the variety standard:** the person's true top three tones
    at 60/20/20. No qualifying method can beat this, whatever information it
    uses.
-   **Best fixed qualifying method:** the sample's top three tones at 60/20/20.
    No method that ignores the individual can beat this.

```{r}
#| label: Ceiling
ceiling_table <- imap(style_data, \(s, nm) {
  mu <- colMeans(s$M)
  mu_sorted <- sort(mu, decreasing = TRUE)
  true_values <- matrix(rnorm(n_sim * 5, 0, s$sd_person_tone), ncol = 5) +
    matrix(mu, nrow = n_sim, ncol = 5, byrow = TRUE)
  sorted <- t(apply(true_values, 1, sort, decreasing = TRUE))
  tibble(
    styles = nm,
    uniform = mean(mu),
    best_fixed_qualifying = sum(c(.6, .2, .2) * mu_sorted[1:3]),
    mean_only = mu_sorted[[1]],
    oracle_with_variety = mean(sorted[, 1] * .6 + sorted[, 2] * .2 + sorted[, 3] * .2),
    oracle_no_constraint = mean(sorted[, 1]),
    in_sample_best_case = mean(apply(s$M, 1, max)))
}) |> list_rbind()
ceiling_table
```

Reading this table:

-   If `best_fixed_qualifying` is below 5.5, **no fixed rotation that meets
    the variety standard can reach 5.5** in this sample.
-   If `oracle_with_variety` is below or near 5.5, the target is out of reach
    under the variety standard even with perfect knowledge of every person.
-   The gap between `best_fixed_qualifying` and `oracle_with_variety` is the
    most that individual information (preferences, demographics, or ratings
    collected in use) could ever add under the standard.

A target expressed as `retained` (share of mean-only's gain kept) or as a
share of the distance from uniform to `oracle_with_variety` is reachable and
means the same thing in both style settings. An absolute target is not.

# 5. Selecting a Method

Proposed rule, applied separately to each style setting:

1.  Keep only methods that meet the variety standard.
2.  Find the best held-out mean among them.
3.  Keep methods within `margin` points of it. These are treated as equally
    helpful on average; the differences are within noise.
4.  Among those, choose the lowest `pct_worse_off`.
5.  If two are still level, prefer the simpler one (a fixed method over a
    preference-based one, fewer rules over more).

```{r}
#| label: Selection
selection <- imap(results, \(r, nm) {
  r |>
    filter(qualifies) |>
    mutate(styles = nm,
           best_mean = max(held_out_mean),
           within_margin = held_out_mean >= best_mean - margin,
           selected = within_margin &
             pct_worse_off == min(pct_worse_off[within_margin], na.rm = TRUE)) |>
    arrange(desc(within_margin), pct_worse_off) |>
    select(styles, method, held_out_mean, retained, diff_vs_mean_only, diff_low,
           diff_high, pct_worse_off, pct_clearly_worse, within_margin, selected)
}) |> list_rbind()

selection |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3))) |>
  print(n = Inf, width = Inf)

selection |> filter(selected) |> select(styles, method, held_out_mean, retained, pct_worse_off)
```

Things to check before trusting the selection:

-   Does the same method win in both style settings? If not, the candidates
    in the margin are effectively tied and step 5 should decide.
-   Does the norms variant beat plain "own order"? That is the test of whether
    the norms rule earns its place.
-   `margin` and `harm_threshold` are judgment calls set in the Settings
    chunk. Re-run with other values to see whether the choice is stable.

# 6. Do the Preference-Based Methods Actually Personalize?

If most people state the same preference order, "own order" would hand nearly
everyone the same rotation as the fixed method, and calling it
preference-based would be misleading. This section checks what people would
actually receive. Weights use the full-sample tone ranking (pooled styles).

```{r}
#| label: Assignment Profiles
# rotation_label() (functions_assignment.R) gives one label per respondent describing
# their rotation, e.g. "SE 50 / VA 30 / Leg 20"

compare_to <- "Top three, 50/30/20"
W_fixed <- methods[[compare_to]](top_full, seq_len(n))
fixed_label <- rotation_label(W_fixed[1, ])
fixed_label

pref_methods <- c("Own order, 50/30/20", "Own order, 50/30/20 + norms",
                  "Own order, 50/30/20 + norms, sample tiebreak",
                  "Own top three, 50/30/20", "Rule-based")

W_full <- map(set_names(pref_methods), \(nm) methods[[nm]](top_full, seq_len(n)))

personalization <- imap(W_full, \(W, nm) {
  labels <- apply(W, 1, rotation_label)
  tibble(
    method = nm,
    distinct_rotations = n_distinct(labels),
    pct_same_as_fixed = mean(labels == fixed_label),
    # share of a person's messages that differ in tone from the fixed rotation
    pct_messages_reallocated = mean(rowSums(abs(W - W_fixed)) / 2),
    pct_same_top_tone_as_fixed = mean(W[, top_full[1]] == apply(W, 1, max) &
                                        rowSums(W == apply(W, 1, max)) == 1),
    pct_receiving_norms = mean(W[, "norms"] > 0),
    pct_receiving_acknowledging = mean(W[, "acknowledging"] > 0))
}) |> list_rbind()
personalization |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

How to read it:

-   `pct_same_as_fixed`: share of respondents whose rotation is identical to
    the fixed 50/30/20. If this is high, the method is the fixed method in
    effect.
-   `pct_messages_reallocated`: on average, the share of a person's messages
    that would be in a different tone than under the fixed rotation.
-   `pct_same_top_tone_as_fixed`: share whose single most-seen tone is the
    sample's top tone.

*Most common rotations under each preference-based method*

```{r}
#| label: Rotation Counts
imap(W_full, \(W, nm) {
  tibble(method = nm, rotation = apply(W, 1, rotation_label)) |>
    count(method, rotation, sort = TRUE) |>
    mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) |>
    slice_head(n = 8)
}) |> list_rbind() |>
  mutate(pct = round(pct, 3)) |>
  print(n = Inf)
```

*Average share of messages in each tone*

Even when individuals differ, the average mix across the sample may look like
the fixed rotation. That is expected and is not the same as everyone getting
the same thing.

```{r}
#| label: Average Mix
c(list(W_fixed) |> set_names(compare_to), W_full) |>
  imap(\(W, nm) as_tibble_row(colMeans(W)) |> mutate(method = nm, .before = 1)) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

# 7. Paired Comparisons Between Candidates

Each comparison is A minus B on held-out expected ratings, paired within
respondent, with a 95% bootstrap interval and Cohen's dz. `n_affected` is the
number of respondents whose rotation differs between the two methods, and
`diff_affected` is the mean difference among just those respondents (the rest
contribute exactly zero).

```{r}
#| label: Paired Comparisons
comparisons <- tribble(
  ~question,                                        ~a,                            ~b,
  "Best preference-based vs. simplest fixed",       "Own order, 50/30/20 + norms", "Top three, 40/40/20",
  "Does preference ordering help? (same weights)",  "Own order, 50/30/20",         "Top three, 50/30/20",
  "Does the norms rule help?",                      "Own order, 50/30/20 + norms", "Own order, 50/30/20",
  "Own tone set vs. the sample's tone set",         "Own top three, 50/30/20",     "Own order, 50/30/20",
  "Own tone set vs. simplest fixed",                "Own top three, 50/30/20",     "Top three, 40/40/20",
  "Own order + norms vs. rule-based",               "Own order, 50/30/20 + norms", "Rule-based",
  "Tiebreak by sample order vs. shared weights",    "Own order, 50/30/20 + norms, sample tiebreak", "Own order, 50/30/20 + norms",
  "Tiebreak version vs. simplest fixed",            "Own order, 50/30/20 + norms, sample tiebreak", "Top three, 40/40/20",
  "Tiebreak version vs. fixed 50/30/20",            "Own order, 50/30/20 + norms, sample tiebreak", "Top three, 50/30/20")

paired <- imap(evaluated, \(e, style_nm) {
  pmap(comparisons, \(question, a, b) {
    d <- e$values[, a] - e$values[, b]
    affected <- rowSums(abs(e$weights[[a]] - e$weights[[b]])) > 1e-9
    boot <- map_dbl(seq_len(n_boot), \(i) mean(sample(d, replace = TRUE)))
    tibble(styles = style_nm, question = question, a = a, b = b,
           diff = mean(d),
           ci_low = quantile(boot, .025), ci_high = quantile(boot, .975),
           dz = mean(d) / sd(d),
           p = t.test(d)$p.value,
           n_affected = sum(affected),
           diff_affected = mean(d[affected]))
  }) |> list_rbind()
}) |> list_rbind()

paired |>
  mutate(across(c(diff, ci_low, ci_high, dz, diff_affected), \(x) round(x, 3)),
         p = round(p, 4)) |>
  select(styles, question, diff, ci_low, ci_high, dz, p, n_affected, diff_affected) |>
  print(n = Inf, width = Inf)
```

Reading the results:

-   An interval that includes zero means the two methods cannot be told apart
    on mean helpfulness. In that case the choice rests on other grounds
    (variety, fairness, simplicity).
-   An interval entirely below zero for "Own tone set vs. ..." means that
    relying on each person's own preferred tones costs helpfulness, which is
    what the preference-reliability results would predict.

# 8. Method Refinements: Ties and the Norms Rule

```{r}
#| label: Lead Candidates
# The lead candidates compared in Sections 8 to 11 (from robustness_analyses.qmd)
lead_method <- "Own order, 50/30/20 + norms"
fixed_method <- "Top three, 40/40/20"
alt_method <- "Own top three, 50/30/20"
tiebreak_method <- "Own order, 50/30/20 + norms, sample tiebreak"

# Mean, gain, SD of true gains, and the shares worse off and clearly worse off, from
# method_metrics() in functions_assignment.R
metrics <- function(e, nm, idx = seq_len(n)) {
  method_metrics(e, nm, e$sd_resid, e$n_per_tone, harm_threshold, idx)[
    c("mean", "gain", "sd_gain", "pct_worse", "pct_clearly")]
}
```

## Tie and norms rules

From `final_checks.qmd`. The methods here are scored separately from Sections 1 to 7
(objects prefixed `refine_`), on the same cross-validation folds.

The candidates differ on two switches.

**Tie rule** (what happens when a person's stated preferences among the three
tones are tied):

-   *shared*: tied tones split their weights (three tied gives equal thirds).
-   *sample*: tied tones are ordered by the sample ranking.
-   *middle*: sample ranking only when all three are tied; partial ties share.

**Norms rule** (when norms replaces the third tone):

-   *tier*: norms is in the person's highest preference tier (ties count).
-   *strict*: norms is preferred strictly above every other tone.
-   *none*: never.

```{r}
#| label: Refinement Methods
# Re-set the seed so these folds and the bootstraps below match final_checks.qmd exactly
# (the folds were its first random draw). final_checks.qmd used 1,000 bootstrap resamples.
set.seed(102030)
n_boot <- 1000

w <- c(.50, .30, .20)
refine_methods <- list(
  "Mean-only"                      = fixed(1),
  "Fixed 40/40/20"                 = fixed(c(.40, .40, .20)),
  "Fixed 50/30/20"                 = fixed(w),
  "Uniform (all five)"             = fixed(rep(1 / 5, 5)),
  "Shared ties, norms tier"        = own_order(w, norms = "tier", ties = "share"),
  "Sample ties, norms tier"        = own_order(w, norms = "tier", ties = "sample"),
  "Middle ties, norms tier"        = own_order(w, norms = "tier", ties = "sample_if_all_tied"),
  "Shared ties, norms strict"      = own_order(w, norms = "strict", ties = "share"),
  "Sample ties, norms strict"      = own_order(w, norms = "strict", ties = "sample"),
  "Middle ties, norms strict"      = own_order(w, norms = "strict", ties = "sample_if_all_tied"),
  "Shared ties, no norms"          = own_order(w, norms = "none", ties = "share"),
  "Sample ties, no norms"          = own_order(w, norms = "none", ties = "sample"),
  "Middle ties, no norms"          = own_order(w, norms = "none", ties = "sample_if_all_tied"))

lead_shared <- "Shared ties, norms tier"   # the current lead in the report
lead_sample <- "Sample ties, norms tier"   # the tiebreak version
lead_middle <- "Middle ties, norms tier"
refine_pref_methods <- str_subset(names(refine_methods), "ties")

folds <- make_respondent_folds(n, cv_folds, cv_repeats)
refine_evaluated <- map(style_data, \(s) {
  c(evaluate_methods(refine_methods, s$M, folds, cv_repeats),
    list(sd_resid = s$sd_resid, n_per_tone = s$n_per_tone))
})

# The metrics this script reports, from method_metrics() in functions_assignment.R
refine_metrics <- function(e, nm, idx = seq_len(n)) {
  method_metrics(e, nm, e$sd_resid, e$n_per_tone, harm_threshold, idx)[
    c("mean", "gain", "pct_worse", "pct_clearly", "pct_worse_raw")]
}
```

*Every candidate meets the variety standard?*

```{r}
#| label: Refinement Variety Check
top_full <- names(sort(colMeans(style_data[["Pooled styles"]]$M), decreasing = TRUE))
map(set_names(refine_pref_methods), \(nm) {
  W <- refine_methods[[nm]](top_full, seq_len(n))
  tibble(tones_min = min(rowSums(W > 0)), least_seen = min(apply(W, 1, \(x) min(x[x > 0]))))
}) |> list_rbind(names_to = "method")
```

## How many people each rule affects

```{r}
#| label: Rule Reach
# How many respondents each rule touches: norms in the highest preference tier, norms
# strictly highest, all three top tones tied, any tie among them. Then, for each
# preference-based method, how far its rotations depart from the fixed 50/30/20 rotation.
tibble(
  norms_tier = apply(P, 1, \(p) p[["norms"]] == max(p) && min(p) < max(p)),
  norms_strict = apply(P, 1, \(p) p[["norms"]] > max(p[names(p) != "norms"])),
  three_tied = apply(P[, top_full[1:3]], 1, \(p) n_distinct(p) == 1),
  any_tie = apply(P[, top_full[1:3]], 1, \(p) n_distinct(p) < 3)) |>
  summarise(across(everything(), list(n = sum, pct = mean))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = c("rule", ".value"), names_pattern = "(.*)_(n|pct)$")

W_fixed <- refine_methods[["Fixed 50/30/20"]](top_full, seq_len(n))
fixed_label <- rotation_label(W_fixed[1, ])

map(set_names(refine_pref_methods), \(nm) {
  W <- refine_methods[[nm]](top_full, seq_len(n))
  labels <- apply(W, 1, rotation_label)
  tibble(distinct_rotations = n_distinct(labels),
         pct_same_as_fixed = mean(labels == fixed_label),
         pct_messages_reallocated = mean(rowSums(abs(W - W_fixed)) / 2),
         pct_receiving_norms = mean(W[, "norms"] > 0))
}) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "method") |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

## Held-out performance

Share worse off than an even rotation is noise-corrected (see Section 3), with the uncorrected share alongside. Intervals for
the corrected share come from a respondent bootstrap.

```{r}
#| label: Refinement Results
refine_results <- imap(refine_evaluated, \(e, style_nm) {
  map(set_names(names(refine_methods)), \(nm) {
    obs <- refine_metrics(e, nm)
    boot <- replicate(n_boot, refine_metrics(e, nm, sample(n, replace = TRUE))[["pct_worse"]])
    tibble(mean = obs[["mean"]],
           retained = obs[["gain"]] / refine_metrics(e, "Mean-only")[["gain"]],
           pct_worse = obs[["pct_worse"]],
           worse_low = quantile(boot, .025, na.rm = TRUE),
           worse_high = quantile(boot, .975, na.rm = TRUE),
           pct_clearly = obs[["pct_clearly"]],
           pct_worse_raw = obs[["pct_worse_raw"]])
  }) |>
    list_rbind(names_to = "method") |>
    mutate(styles = style_nm, .before = 1)
}) |> list_rbind()

refine_results |>
  arrange(styles, desc(mean)) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3))) |>
  print(n = Inf, width = Inf)
```

## Paired comparisons

A minus B on held-out expected ratings, with 95% bootstrap intervals.
`n_affected` is the number of respondents whose rotation differs between the
two, and `diff_affected` the mean difference among them.

```{r}
#| label: Refinement Comparisons
comparisons <- tribble(
  ~question,                                   ~a,                          ~b,
  "Tie rule: sample vs. shared",               "Sample ties, norms tier",   "Shared ties, norms tier",
  "Tie rule: middle vs. shared",               "Middle ties, norms tier",   "Shared ties, norms tier",
  "Tie rule: sample vs. middle",               "Sample ties, norms tier",   "Middle ties, norms tier",
  "Norms rule: tier vs. none (sample ties)",   "Sample ties, norms tier",   "Sample ties, no norms",
  "Norms rule: strict vs. none (sample ties)", "Sample ties, norms strict", "Sample ties, no norms",
  "Norms rule: tier vs. strict (sample ties)", "Sample ties, norms tier",   "Sample ties, norms strict",
  "Norms rule: tier vs. none (shared ties)",   "Shared ties, norms tier",   "Shared ties, no norms",
  "Middle path vs. fixed 40/40/20",            "Middle ties, norms tier",   "Fixed 40/40/20",
  "Middle path vs. fixed 50/30/20",            "Middle ties, norms tier",   "Fixed 50/30/20",
  "Sample ties vs. fixed 50/30/20",            "Sample ties, norms tier",   "Fixed 50/30/20",
  "Shared ties vs. fixed 50/30/20",            "Shared ties, norms tier",   "Fixed 50/30/20")

refine_paired <- imap(refine_evaluated, \(e, style_nm) {
  pmap(comparisons, \(question, a, b) {
    d <- e$values[, a] - e$values[, b]
    affected <- rowSums(abs(e$weights[[a]] - e$weights[[b]])) > 1e-9
    boot <- replicate(n_boot, mean(sample(d, replace = TRUE)))
    tibble(styles = style_nm, question = question,
           diff = mean(d), ci_low = quantile(boot, .025), ci_high = quantile(boot, .975),
           p = t.test(d)$p.value, n_affected = sum(affected),
           diff_affected = if (any(affected)) mean(d[affected]) else NA_real_)
  }) |> list_rbind()
}) |> list_rbind()

refine_paired |>
  mutate(across(c(diff, ci_low, ci_high, diff_affected), \(x) round(x, 3)), p = round(p, 4)) |>
  print(n = Inf, width = Inf)
```

Reading the results:

-   **Middle vs. shared, and sample vs. middle**, show where the tiebreak's
    gain comes from: people who tied all three tones, or people with a partial
    tie. If the middle path captures most of the gain, it is the option that
    costs the least personalization.
-   **Norms tier vs. strict** shows whether the people with the clearest norms
    preference account for the rule's benefit. A strict rule that does as well
    while sending norms to fewer people is the safer rule.

## By preference pattern

From `robustness_analyses.qmd`.

The lead method gives equal thirds to anyone who scored its three tones the
same. Does it serve those respondents worse than people who expressed a clear
order? And does it beat the fixed method for people who did express one?

```{r}
#| label: Preference Patterns
patterns <- tibble(
  subid = ids,
  all_five_tied = apply(P, 1, \(p) n_distinct(p) == 1),
  top_three_distinct = apply(P[, top_full[1:3]], 1, n_distinct),
  norms_swapped = apply(P, 1, \(p) p[["norms"]] == max(p) && min(p) < max(p))) |>
  mutate(pattern = case_when(
    all_five_tied ~ "All five tones tied",
    norms_swapped ~ "Norms ranked highest",
    top_three_distinct == 1 ~ "Top three tied (others differ)",
    top_three_distinct == 2 ~ "Partial order (one tie)",
    top_three_distinct == 3 ~ "Full order"))
patterns |> count(pattern) |> mutate(pct = n / sum(n))

imap(evaluated, \(e, style_nm) {
  patterns |>
    mutate(uniform = e$uniform,
           gain_fixed = e$values[, fixed_method] - uniform,
           gain_lead = e$values[, lead_method] - uniform,
           gain_alt = e$values[, alt_method] - uniform,
           gain_tiebreak = e$values[, tiebreak_method] - uniform,
           tiebreak_minus_fixed = e$values[, tiebreak_method] - e$values[, fixed_method],
           lead_minus_fixed = e$values[, lead_method] - e$values[, fixed_method]) |>
    summarise(n = n(), mean_rating_overall = mean(uniform),
              across(c(gain_fixed, gain_lead, gain_tiebreak, gain_alt), mean),
              tiebreak_diff = mean(tiebreak_minus_fixed),
              tiebreak_diff_low = tiebreak_diff -
                1.96 * sd(tiebreak_minus_fixed) / sqrt(n()),
              tiebreak_diff_high = tiebreak_diff +
                1.96 * sd(tiebreak_minus_fixed) / sqrt(n()),
              diff = mean(lead_minus_fixed),
              diff_low = diff - 1.96 * sd(lead_minus_fixed) / sqrt(n()),
              diff_high = diff + 1.96 * sd(lead_minus_fixed) / sqrt(n()),
              .by = pattern) |>
    mutate(styles = style_nm, .before = 1)
}) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3))) |>
  arrange(styles, desc(n)) |>
  print(n = Inf, width = Inf)
```

`diff` is lead minus fixed 40/40/20 within each pattern, and `tiebreak_diff`
is the same for the sample-tiebreak version of the lead method. The lead method can
only add value where it changes the rotation, so expect its advantage (if
any) among "Full order", "Partial order" and "Norms ranked highest".

# 9. Fairness

Three views of who benefits: descriptive gains by group (from
`candidate_methods.qmd`), tests of those gaps (from `robustness_analyses.qmd`), and
tests for every lead candidate (from `final_checks.qmd`).

## Who benefits? Results by demographic group

A fixed rotation is built from what the whole sample rated highest, and the
sample is mostly White and male. If a fixed method served the majority better
than everyone else, that would be a reason to prefer a preference-based
method even at equal average helpfulness. For each group this shows the mean
gain over an even rotation under several methods, and the paired difference
between the leading preference-based and fixed methods.

Small groups have wide intervals. Read this as a check for large disparities,
not as a test of small ones.

```{r}
#| label: By Demographic
dems <- panel_long |>
  distinct(subid, dem_sex, dem_ethnicity, dem_orientation, dem_education,
           dem_minority, dem_age) |>
  arrange(subid) |>
  mutate(age_group = cut(dem_age, breaks = quantile(dem_age, c(0, 1 / 3, 2 / 3, 1), na.rm = TRUE),
                         include.lowest = TRUE)) |>
  select(-dem_age) |>
  mutate(across(-subid, as.character))
stopifnot(identical(dems$subid, ids))

show_methods <- c("Mean-only", "Top three, 40/40/20", "Top three, 50/30/20",
                  "Own order, 50/30/20", "Own order, 50/30/20 + norms",
                  "Own top three, 50/30/20")
pref_method <- "Own order, 50/30/20 + norms"
fixed_method <- "Top three, 40/40/20"

by_group <- imap(evaluated, \(e, style_nm) {
  gains <- as_tibble(e$values[, show_methods] - e$uniform)
  d <- e$values[, pref_method] - e$values[, fixed_method]
  bind_cols(dems, gains, pref_minus_fixed = d) |>
    pivot_longer(c(dem_sex, dem_ethnicity, dem_orientation, dem_education,
                   dem_minority, age_group),
                 names_to = "variable", values_to = "level") |>
    drop_na(level) |>
    summarise(n = n(),
              across(all_of(show_methods), mean),
              pref_minus_fixed_se = sd(pref_minus_fixed) / sqrt(n()),
              pref_minus_fixed = mean(pref_minus_fixed),
              .by = c(variable, level)) |>
    mutate(styles = style_nm, .before = 1) |>
    mutate(ci_low = pref_minus_fixed - 1.96 * pref_minus_fixed_se,
           ci_high = pref_minus_fixed + 1.96 * pref_minus_fixed_se) |>
    select(-pref_minus_fixed_se)
}) |> list_rbind()

by_group |>
  filter(styles == "Pooled styles") |>
  arrange(variable, desc(n)) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3))) |>
  print(n = Inf, width = Inf)

by_group |>
  filter(styles == "Informal only") |>
  arrange(variable, desc(n)) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3))) |>
  print(n = Inf, width = Inf)
```

*Spread between groups*

For each variable and method, the difference between the best- and
worst-served group (groups with at least 30 respondents). A smaller spread
means the method's benefit is shared more evenly.

```{r}
#| label: Group Spread
by_group |>
  filter(n >= 30) |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(show_methods), names_to = "method", values_to = "gain") |>
  summarise(spread = max(gain) - min(gain), min_gain = min(gain), groups = n(),
            .by = c(styles, variable, method)) |>
  select(-min_gain) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = method, values_from = spread) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3))) |>
  print(n = Inf, width = Inf)
```

One caution on interpretation: "own order" still takes its three tones from
the sample ranking; only the order is personal. "Own top three" is the only
candidate whose tone set is personal too.

## Demographic gaps, tested

The gaps reported so far are descriptive. Two questions for each grouping:

-   **Does the method benefit groups unequally?** A one-way test of the gain
    (method minus an even rotation) across groups.
-   **Does the preference-based method change the gap?** The paired difference
    (lead method minus fixed method, and lead minus mean-only) across groups.
    A significant result means the two methods distribute their benefit
    differently.

AUDIT group is included alongside the demographic variables. p-values are
adjusted across groupings within each column (Benjamini-Hochberg). Levels with
fewer than 30 respondents are dropped.

```{r}
#| label: Group Data
# AUDIT zone for each respondent (also built in robustness_checks.qmd)
audit <- raw_panel |>
  transmute(subid, audit_score,
            audit_group = cut(audit_score, breaks = c(-Inf, 15, 19, Inf),
                              labels = c("8-15", "16-19", "20+")))

groups <- panel_long |>
  distinct(subid, dem_sex, dem_ethnicity, dem_orientation, dem_education,
           dem_minority, dem_age) |>
  left_join(audit |> select(subid, audit_group), by = "subid") |>
  arrange(subid) |>
  mutate(age_group = cut(dem_age, breaks = quantile(dem_age, c(0, 1 / 3, 2 / 3, 1), na.rm = TRUE),
                         include.lowest = TRUE)) |>
  select(-dem_age) |>
  mutate(across(-subid, as.character))
stopifnot(identical(groups$subid, ids))
group_vars <- setdiff(names(groups), "subid")
```

```{r}
#| label: Group Tests
# One-way test of `y` across the levels of a grouping (levels with n >= 30)
# group_test() is in functions_assignment.R

group_tests <- imap(evaluated, \(e, style_nm) {
  outcomes <- list(
    "Gain: mean-only" = e$values[, "Mean-only"] - e$uniform,
    "Gain: fixed 40/40/20" = e$values[, fixed_method] - e$uniform,
    "Gain: lead (own order + norms)" = e$values[, lead_method] - e$uniform,
    "Gain: alternative (own top three)" = e$values[, alt_method] - e$uniform,
    "Lead minus fixed" = e$values[, lead_method] - e$values[, fixed_method],
    "Lead minus mean-only" = e$values[, lead_method] - e$values[, "Mean-only"])
  imap(outcomes, \(y, out_nm) {
    map(set_names(group_vars), \(v) group_test(y, groups[[v]])) |>
      list_rbind(names_to = "grouping") |>
      mutate(outcome = out_nm, p_bh = p.adjust(p, "BH"))
  }) |>
    list_rbind() |>
    mutate(styles = style_nm, .before = 1)
}) |> list_rbind()

group_tests |>
  mutate(across(c(gap, p, p_bh), \(x) round(x, 3))) |>
  select(styles, outcome, grouping, levels, gap, best, worst, p, p_bh) |>
  arrange(styles, outcome, p) |>
  print(n = Inf, width = Inf)
```

*Gaps side by side*

```{r}
#| label: Group Gap Table
group_tests |>
  filter(str_starts(outcome, "Gain")) |>
  mutate(cell = paste0(sprintf("%.2f", gap), if_else(!is.na(p) & p < .05, "*", ""))) |>
  select(styles, grouping, outcome, cell) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = outcome, values_from = cell) |>
  arrange(styles, grouping) |>
  print(n = Inf, width = Inf)
```

`*` marks an unadjusted p < .05 for unequal benefit across the grouping's
levels.

Reading the results:

-   Gaps for the lead method that are small **and** not significant support
    the claim that it shares its benefit evenly. Absence of a significant gap
    is weak evidence with groups this size; report the gap and its test, not
    "no difference".
-   A significant "Lead minus mean-only" row means the lead method
    redistributes benefit relative to a single tone, the clearest fairness
    result available here.

## Fairness tests for each lead candidate

From `final_checks.qmd`, using the Section 8 refinements.

For each grouping, a one-way test of whether the method's gain over an even
rotation differs across groups (levels with at least 30 respondents), and the
gap between the best- and worst-served group. `p_bh` adjusts across groupings
within a method.

```{r}
#| label: Fairness
groups <- panel_long |>
  distinct(subid, dem_sex, dem_ethnicity, dem_orientation, dem_education,
           dem_minority, dem_age) |>
  left_join(raw_panel |> select(subid, audit_score), by = "subid") |>
  arrange(subid) |>
  mutate(age_group = as.character(cut(dem_age, quantile(dem_age, c(0, 1 / 3, 2 / 3, 1), na.rm = TRUE),
                                      include.lowest = TRUE)),
         audit_group = as.character(cut(audit_score, c(-Inf, 15, 19, Inf),
                                        labels = c("8-15", "16-19", "20+")))) |>
  select(-dem_age, -audit_score) |>
  mutate(across(-subid, as.character))
stopifnot(identical(groups$subid, ids))
group_vars <- setdiff(names(groups), "subid")

# group_test() is in functions_assignment.R; its `levels` column is not used here

fairness_methods <- c("Mean-only", "Fixed 40/40/20", lead_shared, lead_sample, lead_middle)

fairness <- imap(refine_evaluated, \(e, style_nm) {
  map(set_names(fairness_methods), \(nm) {
    map(set_names(group_vars), \(v) {
      group_test(e$values[, nm] - e$uniform, groups[[v]]) |> select(-levels)
    }) |>
      list_rbind(names_to = "grouping") |>
      mutate(p_bh = p.adjust(p, "BH"))
  }) |>
    list_rbind(names_to = "method") |>
    mutate(styles = style_nm, .before = 1)
}) |> list_rbind()

# Gaps side by side (* = unadjusted p < .05)
fairness |>
  mutate(cell = paste0(sprintf("%.2f", gap), if_else(!is.na(p) & p < .05, "*", ""))) |>
  select(styles, grouping, method, cell) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = method, values_from = cell) |>
  arrange(styles, grouping) |>
  print(n = Inf, width = Inf)

# Any grouping with unequal benefit under a lead candidate
fairness |>
  filter(method %in% c(lead_shared, lead_sample, lead_middle), p < .10) |>
  mutate(across(c(gap, p, p_bh), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

*Do the lead candidates distribute benefit differently from each other?*

```{r}
#| label: Fairness Between Leads
imap(refine_evaluated, \(e, style_nm) {
  d <- e$values[, lead_sample] - e$values[, lead_shared]
  map(set_names(group_vars), \(v) group_test(d, groups[[v]]) |> select(-levels)) |>
    list_rbind(names_to = "grouping") |>
    mutate(styles = style_nm, comparison = "Sample ties minus shared ties", .before = 1)
}) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  mutate(across(c(gap, p), \(x) round(x, 3))) |>
  print(n = Inf, width = Inf)
```

# 10. Selection Stability

From `robustness_analyses.qmd`.

## Other selection settings

The selection rule keeps qualifying methods within `margin` of the best
held-out mean, then picks the lowest share worse off. Note that
`harm_threshold` does not enter that rule; it only defines the "clearly worse
off" column. So the grid varies the margin, and separately tries a rule that
picks on the share **clearly** worse off.

```{r}
#| label: Selection Grid
metrics_table <- function(e, idx = seq_len(n)) {
  t(sapply(qualifying, \(nm) metrics(e, nm, idx)))
}
apply_rule <- function(tbl, margin, by = "pct_worse") {
  ok <- tbl[, "mean"] >= max(tbl[, "mean"]) - margin & !is.na(tbl[, by])
  rownames(tbl)[ok][which.min(tbl[ok, by])]
}

expand_grid(styles = names(evaluated),
            margin = c(0, .01, .02, .03, .05, .075, .10),
            by = c("pct_worse", "pct_clearly")) |>
  mutate(selected = pmap_chr(list(styles, margin, by), \(s, m, b) {
    apply_rule(metrics_table(evaluated[[s]]), m, b)
  })) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = margin, values_from = selected, names_prefix = "margin_") |>
  print(width = Inf)
```

## Bootstrap

Respondents are resampled with replacement, every qualifying method is
re-scored, and the rule is re-applied. The table shows how often each method
is selected, and how often it has the best mean outright.

```{r}
#| label: Selection Bootstrap
# Re-set the random stream to where robustness_analyses.qmd had it (just after drawing
# the cross-validation folds), so the bootstrap reproduces the original results exactly.
# That script used 1,000 resamples.
set.seed(102030)
invisible(make_respondent_folds(n, cv_folds, cv_repeats))
n_boot <- 1000

selection_boot <- imap(evaluated, \(e, style_nm) {
  map(seq_len(n_boot), \(i) {
    tbl <- metrics_table(e, sample(n, replace = TRUE))
    tibble(selected = apply_rule(tbl, margin),
           best_mean = rownames(tbl)[which.max(tbl[, "mean"])])
  }) |>
    list_rbind() |>
    mutate(styles = style_nm)
}) |> list_rbind()

full_join(
  selection_boot |> count(styles, method = selected, name = "selected") |>
    mutate(pct_selected = selected / n_boot),
  selection_boot |> count(styles, method = best_mean, name = "best") |>
    mutate(pct_best_mean = best / n_boot),
  by = c("styles", "method")) |>
  select(styles, method, pct_selected, pct_best_mean) |>
  mutate(across(starts_with("pct"), \(x) replace_na(x, 0))) |>
  arrange(styles, desc(pct_selected)) |>
  print(n = Inf)

# How often a preference-based method (any of them) is selected
pref_based <- c("Own order, 50/30/20", "Own order, 40/40/20",
                "Own order, 50/30/20, sample tiebreak",
                "Own order, 50/30/20 + norms, sample tiebreak",
                "Own order, 50/30/20 + norms", "Own top three, 50/30/20", "Rule-based")
selection_boot |>
  summarise(pct_preference_based = mean(selected %in% pref_based), .by = styles)
```

The bootstrap resamples respondents but keeps the cross-validation folds
fixed, so it slightly understates the uncertainty.

Reading the results: if the lead method is selected in well under half of
resamples, describe it as "one of several equivalent methods, chosen on
fairness grounds", not as the winner of a selection procedure. The last table
is the more robust statement: how often some preference-based method wins.

# 11. Normality Check for the "Worse Off" Metric

From `robustness_analyses.qmd`.

The share worse off assumes each method's true gains are roughly normal. This
compares the observed gains with a normal distribution and reports skewness
and excess kurtosis. Observed gains include rating noise (which is close to
normal), so strong skew here would be a warning.

```{r}
#| label: Normality
check_methods <- c("Mean-only", fixed_method, lead_method, alt_method)

gains_long <- imap(evaluated, \(e, style_nm) {
  map(set_names(check_methods), \(nm) tibble(gain = e$values[, nm] - e$uniform)) |>
    list_rbind(names_to = "method") |>
    mutate(styles = style_nm)
}) |> list_rbind()

gains_long |>
  summarise(mean = mean(gain), sd = sd(gain),
            skewness = mean((gain - mean(gain))^3) / sd(gain)^3,
            excess_kurtosis = mean((gain - mean(gain))^4) / sd(gain)^4 - 3,
            pct_below_zero_observed = mean(gain < 0),
            pct_below_zero_normal = pnorm(0, mean(gain), sd(gain)),
            .by = c(styles, method)) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))

gains_long |>
  ggplot(aes(sample = gain)) +
  stat_qq(size = 0.6) +
  stat_qq_line(color = "firebrick") +
  facet_grid(styles ~ method, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "Normal quantiles", y = "Observed gain over an even rotation")
```

If `pct_below_zero_observed` and `pct_below_zero_normal` agree to within a
couple of points and the points follow the line, the normal assumption is
adequate for the observed gains, and the noise-corrected shares can be
reported as estimates. If they diverge, report the corrected shares as
approximate and give the raw shares alongside.

# 12. Stricter Exclusion

From `final_checks.qmd`. Reported in Section 7.11 of the write-up; kept here
because it summarises the Section 8 method results for the no-flag respondents.

The final sample keeps respondents with a suspicion index of 0 or 1. This
repeats the headline results using only respondents with no flag at all. If
the conclusions hold, they do not depend on where the exclusion line was
drawn.

```{r}
#| label: Stricter Exclusion
flags <- raw_panel |> select(subid, suspicion_index) |> arrange(subid)
stopifnot(identical(flags$subid, ids))
flags |> count(suspicion_index)

clean_rows <- which(flags$suspicion_index == 0)
clean_ids <- ids[clean_rows]
length(clean_rows)

# Tone means and the style gap
bind_rows(
  panel_long |> mutate(sample = "All retained"),
  panel_long |> filter(subid %in% clean_ids) |> mutate(sample = "No flags")) |>
  summarise(rating = mean(rating_num), .by = c(sample, subid, tone)) |>
  summarise(mean = mean(rating), .by = c(sample, tone)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = sample, values_from = mean) |>
  arrange(desc(`All retained`)) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2)))

bind_rows(
  panel_long |> mutate(sample = "All retained"),
  panel_long |> filter(subid %in% clean_ids) |> mutate(sample = "No flags")) |>
  summarise(rating = mean(rating_num), .by = c(sample, subid, style)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = style, values_from = rating) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            p = t.test(informal, formal, paired = TRUE)$p.value,
            gap = mean(informal - formal),
            mean_formal = mean(formal), mean_informal = mean(informal),
            .by = sample) |>
  relocate(p, .after = last_col())
```

```{r}
#| label: Stricter Exclusion Methods
# Held-out method values were computed with everyone; here they are summarised for
# the no-flag respondents only.
key_methods <- c("Uniform (all five)", "Fixed 40/40/20", "Fixed 50/30/20",
                 lead_shared, lead_middle, lead_sample, "Mean-only")

imap(refine_evaluated, \(e, style_nm) {
  map(set_names(key_methods), \(nm) {
    tibble(all_retained = mean(e$values[, nm]),
           no_flags = mean(e$values[clean_rows, nm]),
           worse_all = refine_metrics(e, nm)[["pct_worse"]],
           worse_no_flags = refine_metrics(e, nm, clean_rows)[["pct_worse"]])
  }) |>
    list_rbind(names_to = "method") |>
    mutate(styles = style_nm, .before = 1)
}) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3))) |>
  print(n = Inf, width = Inf)

# Key paired differences among no-flag respondents
imap(refine_evaluated, \(e, style_nm) {
  tribble(~a, ~b,
          lead_sample, "Fixed 40/40/20",
          lead_sample, lead_shared,
          lead_shared, "Fixed 40/40/20",
          lead_sample, "Mean-only") |>
    pmap(\(a, b) {
      d <- e$values[clean_rows, a] - e$values[clean_rows, b]
      tibble(styles = style_nm, a = a, b = b, diff = mean(d),
             ci_low = t.test(d)$conf.int[1], ci_high = t.test(d)$conf.int[2])
    }) |> list_rbind()
}) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3))) |>
  print(width = Inf)
```
